name: ZF 9HP48
fullName: ZF 9HP48 nine-speed transverse automatic (dog clutches A and F, multi-plate B, C, D, E; four planetary sets)
summary: A compact transverse nine-speed with four nested planetary sets and six shift elements, two of them hydraulically moved dog clutches with no friction to absorb a bad engagement. The pump sits off-axis in the bell housing, driven by chain, and there is no bottom pan: everything is reached through a plastic side cover and by splitting the bell housing from the case. Clutch clearances are set with selective rings and plates under a fixed load, and the job is not finished until the TCM is updated and its adaptations relearned.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: Front-transverse 9-speed planetary automatic with lock-up torque converter; AWD via a PTU on the differential side

facts.label: Generation
facts.value: First-generation 9HP48 (L550 Discovery Sport 2015MY on); 9HP50 takes over with the 2020MY facelift

facts.label: Gears
facts.value: 4.700 (1st) to 0.479 (9th), reverse 3.805, from four nested planetary sets

facts.label: Shift elements
facts.value: Dog clutches A and F; friction clutches B and E; friction brakes C and D

facts.label: Oil pump
facts.value: Chain-driven, off-axis dual-chamber vane pump in the bell housing

facts.label: Valve body
facts.value: Inside the case behind a ribbed plastic side cover; 9 solenoids, 10 with electronic park; no bottom pan

facts.label: Mechatronic
facts.value: No: the TCM is a separate module bolted to the outside of the case

facts.label: Fluid level check
facts.value: Engine idling in P, fluid temperature read on the JLR tool, level set at the check plug; JLR's temperature window not found publicly

facts.label: Overhaul fill
facts.value: About 6.5 L of ZF LifeguardFluid 9 (JLR LR023288)

facts.label: Front differential
facts.value: Inside the transmission case on tapered roller bearings; carrier built for 2WD or AWD

facts.label: Clutch clearances
facts.value: B 0.050–0.070 in, C 0.030–0.045 in, D 0.040–0.059 in, E 0.050–0.070 in under 45 lb (smaller packs differ)

facts.label: Start-stop
facts.value: Filter bypass tube gives instant pressure on restart instead of an auxiliary pump

facts.label: Warranty
facts.value: US extension to 5 yr/62,500 mi for 2015MY Discovery Sport and 2014–15 Evoque only

notes: Correction to a common description: the 9HP48 is not an 8HP-style mechatronic. The valve body sits inside the case behind a plastic side cover and the TCM is a separate module bolted to the outside of the case. There is no bottom oil pan; the side cover is the 'pan' and the filter is internal.

Be honest about the job: JLR does not overhaul these. Its bulletins say to update TCM software, fix leaks and low fluid, and otherwise replace the whole transmission. Many 9HP shift complaints were cured by calibration updates and adaptation resets alone, and 2014-2015 Evoque and 2015 Discovery Sport units got an extended US warranty.

Dog clutch problems are the 9HP's signature failure. Common causes are a loose A dog sensing valve screw, worn dog sleeves and splines, and worn A/F dog plunger valve sleeves in the valve body. The usual repair is a complete input shaft assembly plus a valve body plunger kit or a remanufactured valve body, not machining.

The internal sequence here follows Chrysler 948TE service information and trade-press teardowns of the same ZF design. 9HP48 and 948TE parts are not always interchangeable, and torque figures marked '948TE' come from FCA data. Check them against ZF or JLR data for your unit.

Usually replaced: all frictions, every seal, O-ring and gasket, the internal filter, the bell housing gasket and tube seal, differential seals, converter nuts and the gallery plate bolts. Commonly replaced as assemblies: torque converter (sent out or remanufactured), input shaft with A dog if it fails the air test, and the valve body if bores are worn.

Special tools in the factory procedure: a press tool with adapters for the C and D Belleville springs (Miller 8901A, 10428, 10504), a C piston tool (10507A), valve body alignment pins (10379), a force gauge for loading clutch packs during clearance checks, and an arbor press. A JLR diagnostic tool (Pathfinder for 2018MY) is required for the TCM update, configuration and adaptation reset.

Step count is 117, inside the 90-120 target. Not covered step by step: valve body bore-by-bore layout, torque converter internals, and differential/transfer bearing preload, because no public source gives the 9HP48 preload method or values.

Output gear nut torque, converter nut torque, drain/fill plug torques, the JLR fluid-level temperature window and the input shaft end play value are left out because no reliable public source for this unit was found.

phases.name: Diagnosis and removal
phases.summary: Decide whether the unit needs a rebuild at all, then drain it and get it on the bench.

phases.name: External teardown
phases.summary: Strip the converter, controls and bell housing so the geartrain is exposed.

phases.name: Internal teardown
phases.summary: Lift out the final drive, planetaries and C/D brakes, then break down each subassembly.

phases.name: Cleaning and inspection
phases.summary: Clean everything and judge the dog clutches, pump, valve body and bearings.

phases.name: Subassembly rebuild
phases.summary: Rebuild the pump, valve body, rotating clutches and output support before they go back in the case.

phases.name: Case reassembly
phases.summary: Rebuild the case from the bottom up with every clearance checked before the next part covers it.

phases.name: Install, fill and relearn
phases.summary: Refit the unit, fill and level it hot, load software, reset adaptations and road test.

steps.title: Scan codes and software level
steps.action: Read every TCM fault code, record the TCM software level, and note the transmission serial number before touching a wrench.
steps.why: JLR's own guidance ties some 9HP48 codes to serial-number ranges and software levels; that decides whether the box is a rebuild candidate or a reflash.

mistakes.title: Clearing codes before saving them
mistakes.what: Clears the TCM fault memory at the first connection without saving the session, code suffixes or freeze-frame data.
mistakes.consequence: JLR's replace-or-reflash choice depends on the exact codes, so that evidence is lost and an intermittent fault may not come back before teardown.
mistakes.prevent: Save the full diagnostic session, write down every code with its suffix and freeze frame, and only then clear and retest.

mistakes.title: Not recording the transmission serial
mistakes.what: Skips reading the transmission serial number off the case label at the diagnosis stage.
mistakes.consequence: JLR sets replace thresholds by serial number for some codes, and the TCM configure routine needs it later.
mistakes.prevent: Read and photograph the serial label before any work and copy it onto the job card.

mistakes.title: Ignoring body codes that hold Park
mistakes.what: Scans only the TCM when the complaint is a vehicle stuck in Park or that drops back into Park.
mistakes.consequence: Door, hood or hatch ajar signals and an unoccupied driver's seat can keep the shift-by-wire system in Park, so a healthy transmission gets condemned.
mistakes.prevent: Run a full-vehicle scan and clear body faults first; only then treat a no-go or stuck-in-Park as a transmission fault.
mistakes.detect: A body control code for a door, hood, hatch or seat sensor alongside the complaint.

mistakes.title: Skipping the recall and bulletin check
mistakes.what: Starts diagnosis without checking the VIN for open recalls and service actions.
mistakes.consequence: Early neutral-drop and irregular-shift faults fixed by recall software get mistaken for mechanical failure and torn down.
mistakes.prevent: Check the VIN against open recalls and service actions and apply them before judging the hardware.

steps.title: Check level and external leaks
steps.action: Check the fluid level and look for leaks at the valve body cover gasket, case-to-bell-housing joint, cooler joint and the transmission-to-PTU joint.
steps.why: Low fluid alone causes poor shifts, noise and dog clutch codes on this unit; fix the leak before blaming the internals.

mistakes.title: Reading the level cold
mistakes.what: Checks the level at the check plug with cold fluid, the engine off, or without reading fluid temperature on the scan tool.
mistakes.consequence: A cold reading can hide the low fluid behind dog clutch and shift codes, or lead you to overfill.
mistakes.prevent: Check with the engine idling in P and the fluid temperature, read on the scan tool, inside the service window.

mistakes.title: Blaming the wrong leak point
mistakes.what: Assumes fluid at the front of the vehicle is the side cover and ignores the transmission-to-PTU joint and the cooler joint.
mistakes.consequence: The wrong seal gets replaced and the box keeps losing fluid; JLR lists four separate leak points on this unit.
mistakes.prevent: Clean and dry the case, then trace the leak at the cover, case joint, cooler joint and PTU joint.
mistakes.detect: Fresh wetness concentrated at one joint after a short drive on a cleaned case.

mistakes.title: Topping up without fixing the leak
mistakes.what: Tops the fluid back up and returns the vehicle without finding why it was low.
mistakes.consequence: The level falls again; low fluid alone can cause poor shifts, noise, dog clutch codes and even loss of forward gear.
mistakes.prevent: Follow JLR's order: repair leaks, correct the level, update the TCM, then retest.

mistakes.title: Adding leak dye to the fluid
mistakes.what: Puts UV leak-tracing dye into the transmission to find a seep.
mistakes.consequence: It changes the fluid's chemistry, which ZF says not to do, and trade guidance for this family says not to use dye.
mistakes.prevent: Find leaks by cleaning, drying and inspecting instead of additives.

steps.title: Try software and adaptations first
steps.action: If no hard mechanical fault is confirmed, update the TCM to the latest calibration and run the adaptation routine, then road test before committing to a teardown.
steps.why: Many 9HP shift complaints were cured by calibration updates rather than parts; a rebuild will not fix a software complaint.
steps.mistake: Tearing down a box whose only problem was an old calibration.

mistakes.title: Tearing down a software complaint
mistakes.what: Commits to a teardown for harsh, delayed or flared shifts without first loading the latest calibration and relearning adaptations.
mistakes.consequence: The rebuild costs days and parts and the complaint is still there, because many 9HP shift faults were calibration faults.
mistakes.prevent: Update the TCM, reset and relearn adaptations and road test before condemning the hardware.

mistakes.title: Judging before the adaptations have learned
mistakes.what: Drives once after an update or reset and decides the software did nothing.
mistakes.consequence: Each clutch needs repeated shift events before its learned values settle, so early shifts are rough and a good box goes to the bench.
mistakes.prevent: Run the guided adaptation drive and repeat each shift several times before rating shift quality.
mistakes.detect: Adaptation counters still at or near zero on the scan tool.

mistakes.title: Skipping the engine control software check
mistakes.what: Updates the TCM but leaves the engine control module on an old calibration.
mistakes.consequence: The two modules share torque and shift data; the FCA learn procedure for this family requires both at the latest level before learning.
mistakes.prevent: Check and update engine and transmission software together before running any learn.

steps.title: Decide rebuild, swap, or sublet
steps.action: Choose between a full bench overhaul, a valve body or TCM swap, or a replacement unit, based on the codes, fluid debris and what the diagnosis points to.
steps.why: JLR dealers replace the whole transmission for internal faults; an overhaul only makes sense when parts, tooling and service data are in hand.

mistakes.title: Overhauling without tools or data
mistakes.what: Starts a bench overhaul without the C and D spring compressors, a force gauge for clearance checks, or clearance data.
mistakes.consequence: Clearances cannot be set and piston seals get cut, so the job stalls or ends in a replacement unit anyway.
mistakes.prevent: Have the press tools or proven equivalents, a force gauge and the clearance data before the first bolt comes out.

mistakes.title: Ignoring JLR's replace-by-serial guidance
mistakes.what: Plans a soft-parts overhaul on a unit whose code and serial number fall in a range JLR says to replace.
mistakes.consequence: JLR treats those as internal faults beyond a software fix, so a seals-and-frictions job may not reach the root cause.
mistakes.prevent: Compare the stored codes and serial with the bulletins and budget for hard parts or a replacement unit when they match.

mistakes.title: Quoting soft parts for a dog fault
mistakes.what: Prices only a seal and friction kit for a box with dog clutch or no-forward codes.
mistakes.consequence: A failed A dog usually needs a whole input shaft assembly, and worn plunger sleeves need valve body parts, so the job overruns.
mistakes.prevent: Budget for an input shaft assembly, valve body repair parts and a converter when codes point at a dog clutch.

steps.title: Drain fluid and read debris
steps.action: Remove the drain plug, let the fluid drain into a clean pan, and examine it and the plug for metal, friction material and burnt smell.
steps.why: Fine bright metal points toward dog clutch spline damage; friction debris points to a slipping brake or clutch pack.

mistakes.title: Discarding the drain evidence
mistakes.what: Wipes the drain plug and dumps the old fluid without looking at it.
mistakes.consequence: You lose the clue that tells dog spline damage (bright metal) from a slipping pack (friction debris), lengthening the hunt.
mistakes.prevent: Drain into a clean pan, keep a sample in a clear jar and photograph the plug before cleaning it.

mistakes.title: Not planning for a cooler flush
mistakes.what: Finds metal or friction debris in the fluid but does not flag the cooler and lines for flushing or replacement.
mistakes.consequence: Debris trapped in the cooler washes back into the rebuilt unit on first drive.
mistakes.prevent: Write the debris finding on the job card so the cooler is flushed or replaced before the rebuilt unit goes in.

steps.title: Separate halfshafts and PTU
steps.action: With the vehicle supported, remove the front halfshafts and separate the power transfer unit from the transmission's differential side.
steps.why: The US Discovery Sport is AWD, so the PTU is splined into the differential and must come away before the transmission can drop.

mistakes.title: Pushing a halfshaft through the case
mistakes.what: Uses a tool to drive the right-hand halfshaft out through the transmission.
mistakes.consequence: The internal differential sealing plug is knocked out, causing a leak at the differential joint, and may end up inside the case.
mistakes.prevent: Pull halfshafts out from the outboard side only, then check the sealing plug is intact before going further.
mistakes.detect: The differential cross pin is visible through the bore when the plug is missing.

mistakes.title: Levering the PTU off crooked
mistakes.what: Pries the PTU off the differential side at an angle.
mistakes.consequence: The quill shaft seals and retaining clips at the PTU joint get damaged, and that interface becomes a leak point after refit.
mistakes.prevent: Draw the PTU straight off its splines and inspect the quill shaft seals and clips before reuse.

steps.title: Unbolt converter from flexplate
steps.action: Mark the converter-to-flexplate position, turn the engine to reach each fastener, and remove the converter nuts; discard them.
steps.why: JLR requires new flexplate-to-converter nuts on refit, so these are scrap once removed.
steps.mistake: Saving the old converter nuts to reuse on install.

mistakes.title: Saving the converter nuts
mistakes.what: Keeps the flexplate-to-converter nuts to reuse on install.
mistakes.consequence: JLR calls for new nuts and warns that reusing unsuitable fixings leads to later component failures.
mistakes.prevent: Bin the nuts as they come off and order new ones with the rebuild parts.

steps.title: Lower transmission from vehicle
steps.action: Support the engine, disconnect the harness, cooler lines and selector, remove the transmission-to-engine bolts and lower the unit with the converter held in place.
steps.why: The converter can slide off the pump drive as the unit tilts; keep it captured so it does not fall or damage the hub seal.

mistakes.title: Letting the converter slide off
mistakes.what: Lowers the unit nose-down without retaining the converter.
mistakes.consequence: The converter slides off the input shaft and pump drive, damaging the hub seal and possibly the hub or the pump drive gear.
mistakes.prevent: Strap or bracket the converter to the bell housing and keep the unit level on the jack.

steps.title: Wash exterior and mount unit
steps.action: Clean the outside, photograph the bar-code model label on top of the case, then set the transmission on a clean bench or fixture with room to drain.
steps.why: Grime at the cover and bell housing joints falls into the valve body once they open; the label matters because 9HP48 and 948TE parts are not always interchangeable.

mistakes.title: Opening the unit before washing
mistakes.what: Removes the side cover or splits the bell housing before cleaning the outside of the case.
mistakes.consequence: Road grit at the joints falls into the valve body and tube bores, where it scores bores and sticks valves.
mistakes.prevent: Wash the case with solvent or a pressure washer first and work on a clean bench with room to drain.

mistakes.title: Not recording the model label
mistakes.what: Skips photographing the bar-code label and orders parts by vehicle alone.
mistakes.consequence: Park-by-wire and park-by-cable valve bodies and different input shafts exist, so 948TE or wrong-variant parts get fitted.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph the label, decode the exact variant, and match every hard part you order to it.

steps.title: Pull converter and port plugs
steps.action: Slide the converter straight off and drain it face-down, then remove the production fill plug and converter pressure port plugs so the rest of the fluid runs out.
steps.why: The converter must come off first; the bell housing cannot be split with it in place.

mistakes.title: Leaving old fluid in the converter
mistakes.what: Pulls the converter and sets it aside without draining it face-down.
mistakes.consequence: You cannot see what debris it holds, which is the main input to deciding whether the converter is reused or sent out.
mistakes.prevent: Drain the converter into a clean container and look at what comes out.

steps.title: Unbolt the case-mounted TCM
steps.action: Unplug and unbolt the transmission control module from the outside of the case and store it in anti-static packaging.
steps.why: On the 9HP the TCM is a separate module bolted to the case, not built into the valve body as on the 8HP.

mistakes.title: Handling the TCM without static care
mistakes.what: Unbolts the TCM and leaves it on the bench without anti-static packaging, or touches its pins.
mistakes.consequence: A damaged TCM must be replaced, configured to the transmission and relearned, adding parts and time.
mistakes.prevent: Bag the module in anti-static packaging and keep it with the unit.

mistakes.title: Losing track of TCM pairing
mistakes.what: Lets the TCM get separated from its transmission in a shop with several units.
mistakes.consequence: The module holds that unit's configuration and learned values; fitting it to another box gives wrong shift behaviour until it is reconfigured and relearned.
mistakes.prevent: Tag the TCM with the transmission serial number as soon as it comes off.

steps.title: Release the case connector
steps.action: Pull the retaining clip from the main electrical connector and push the connector slightly into the side cover.
steps.why: The connector passes through the cover; it has to be freed before the cover will lift away.

mistakes.title: Lifting the cover with the clip on
mistakes.what: Tries to lift the side cover before pulling the connector clip and pushing the connector inward.
mistakes.consequence: The case connector or its O-rings get torn, and the connector seal leaks after refit.
mistakes.prevent: Pull the clip, push the connector slightly into the cover, and only then lift the cover.

steps.title: Remove valve body side cover
steps.action: Remove the cover bolts (they stay captive in their torque limiters) and lift off the ribbed plastic side cover with its molded seal.
steps.why: There is no bottom pan on the 9HP48; this side cover is the only way into the controls.

mistakes.title: Prying the plastic cover
mistakes.what: Levers the ribbed plastic side cover off at its edge with a screwdriver.
mistakes.consequence: The cover warps or its sealing face is nicked, and the cover joint is JLR's first-listed leak point, causing low fluid, poor shifts and noise.
mistakes.prevent: Release every captive bolt, then lift the cover evenly; plan on the new gasket kit.

mistakes.title: Pulling bolts out of their limiters
mistakes.what: Forces the captive cover bolts out of their torque limiters and loses limiters.
mistakes.consequence: Without limiters the bolts crush the plastic cover on refit, cracking it or distorting the seal.
mistakes.prevent: Leave the bolts captive in the cover and check every limiter is present before refit.

steps.title: Mark solenoids and connector plate
steps.action: Label every solenoid and photograph the connector plate routing before anything is unplugged.
steps.why: The connector plate also carries the speed sensor, range sensor and temperature wiring; reversed solenoids give wrong shifts.
steps.mistake: Pulling solenoids without marking their positions.

mistakes.title: Pulling solenoids without marking them
mistakes.what: Unplugs and removes solenoids without labelling which bore each came from.
mistakes.consequence: Solenoids in the wrong bores apply the wrong elements, giving harsh shifts, wrong gears or a tie-up on the first drive.
mistakes.prevent: Paint-mark each solenoid and its bore and photograph the valve body before anything is unplugged.

mistakes.title: Not photographing the connector plate routing
mistakes.what: Unclips the connector plate wiring without photos of how it runs.
mistakes.consequence: On refit the speed, range and temperature sensor wires get routed where the valve body or cover pinches or chafes them, causing sensor codes.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph the plate and every wire path from two angles before unplugging.

steps.title: Unbolt the valve body
steps.action: Remove only the valve body retaining bolts that hold it to the case; leave the bolts that hold the valve body halves together.
steps.why: Pulling the wrong bolts splits the valve body on the bench and scatters check balls and springs.
steps.mistake: Removing the valve body section bolts along with the mounting bolts.

mistakes.title: Removing the valve body section bolts
mistakes.what: Takes out the bolts that hold the valve body halves together along with the mounting bolts.
mistakes.consequence: The halves separate as the valve body lifts and valves, springs and small parts fall out in unknown order.
mistakes.prevent: Remove only the mounting bolts the service procedure highlights and leave the section bolts alone.

mistakes.title: Mixing valve body bolt lengths
mistakes.what: Drops all the valve body bolts into one tray.
mistakes.consequence: On refit a long bolt in a short hole bottoms out before clamping or damages the casting, and a short one strips threads.
mistakes.prevent: Push the bolts through a cardboard template of the bolt pattern in the order they came out.

mistakes.title: Missing one mounting bolt
mistakes.what: Starts prying the valve body with one mounting bolt still in.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminium valve body casting cracks or bends, which means a replacement valve body.
mistakes.prevent: Count the removed bolts against the service figure before applying any pry force.

steps.title: Pry valve body off tubes
steps.action: Ease the valve body away from the connecting tubes with a suitable pry tool, keeping its harness to the range and speed sensors slack.
steps.why: The tubes carry clutch, converter, pump and lube oil and grip the valve body by their O-rings; the sensor wiring is still attached.
steps.mistake: Yanking the valve body and tearing the range or speed sensor harness.

mistakes.title: Tearing the sensor harness
mistakes.what: Yanks the valve body off its tubes while the range and speed sensor wiring is still attached.
mistakes.consequence: The range or speed sensor harness tears, giving range or speed codes and a sensor replacement.
mistakes.prevent: Keep the harness slack and ease the valve body off a little at a time while watching the wiring.

mistakes.title: Prying on machined faces
mistakes.what: Levers against the valve body's sealing face or the tube bores to free it.
mistakes.consequence: Gouged faces and bores leak at the tube O-rings, robbing a clutch, converter or lube circuit of oil.
mistakes.prevent: Pry only at the proper pry points with a suitable tool and draw the valve body off the tubes squarely.

mistakes.title: Not counting tubes after removal
mistakes.what: Doesn't notice a connecting tube came away inside the valve body instead of staying in the case.
mistakes.consequence: On reassembly the tube is fitted twice or left out, starving the circuit it feeds.
mistakes.prevent: Count the tubes left in the case and any stuck in the valve body before setting it aside.

steps.title: Remove range and speed sensors
steps.action: Unbolt the range sensor and speed sensor from the case and set them aside with the valve body.
steps.why: These sit behind the valve body and can only be reached with it moved.

mistakes.title: Pulling sensors by their wiring
mistakes.what: Works the range or speed sensor out of the case by tugging on its leads.
mistakes.consequence: The sensor or its wiring breaks, adding a part and a fault code after assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Unbolt the sensor and lift it by its body.

steps.title: Pull connecting and bypass tubes
steps.action: Remove the valve body connecting tubes and the filter bypass tube, noting which are round and which have one oblong end.
steps.why: The two oblong-ended tubes feed the output gear support and only fit one way.

mistakes.title: Not recording oblong tube orientation
mistakes.what: Removes the connecting tubes without noting which two have an oblong end and which way it faced.
mistakes.consequence: On refit an oblong tube goes in turned, starving the output gear support circuit that feeds the F dog.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph the tubes in place and lay them out in position order with the oblong ends marked.

mistakes.title: Crushing tube ends with pliers
mistakes.what: Grips the tubes with pliers or vise-grips to pull them out.
mistakes.consequence: The sealing ends go oval and leak at the O-rings even with new seals.
mistakes.prevent: Pull tubes straight by hand or with a padded tool and replace any that are distorted.

mistakes.title: Overlooking the filter bypass tube
mistakes.what: Doesn't note the filter bypass tube as a separate part.
mistakes.consequence: It gets left out on refit, and the unit loses the quick pressure build that lets it drive away promptly after an auto stop.
mistakes.prevent: List every tube, including the bypass tube, on the job card as it comes out.

steps.title: Remove oil gallery plate
steps.action: Unbolt the oil passage cover plate and its bonded steel gasket from the case.
steps.why: This gasket is a known JLR leak point that causes low fluid, noise and poor shifts.

mistakes.title: Gouging the gallery plate face
mistakes.what: Scrapes the bonded gasket residue off with a sharp steel scraper.
mistakes.consequence: A scored case face leaks even with a new gasket, and this joint is a known cause of low fluid, poor shifts and noise.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the face with a plastic scraper and solvent, and inspect it under good light.

steps.title: Remove external hydraulic line
steps.action: Disconnect and remove the external hydraulic line at the back of the case.
steps.why: The line can blow out with age, so it gets inspected and resealed on every overhaul.

mistakes.title: Reusing an aged external line
mistakes.what: Refits the external hydraulic line without inspecting it or renewing its seals.
mistakes.consequence: The line can blow out with age, dumping fluid quickly and leaving the unit to run low.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the line for chafing, corrosion and damaged ends and renew its seals every overhaul.

steps.title: Air-check circuits before teardown
steps.action: With the valve body off, apply regulated shop air to each clutch and dog clutch port and note how each one applies and how much it leaks.
steps.why: A baseline tells you which circuit was leaking; the F dog leaks heavily until its piston shuttles, which is normal.

spec.note: about the minimum air pressure GEARS found needed to shuttle the F dog

mistakes.title: Condemning the F dog for leaking
mistakes.what: Sees the F dog leak heavily on air and writes it off.
mistakes.consequence: Good parts are replaced; the F dog leaks until its piston shuttles and then tightens up, which is normal.
mistakes.prevent: Apply enough regulated air to shuttle the piston and judge the leak after it has moved.
mistakes.detect: The leak drops sharply once the piston has shuttled.

mistakes.title: Skipping the baseline air check
mistakes.what: Tears the unit down without air-checking each circuit first.
mistakes.consequence: There is no record of which circuit was leaking, so the cause of a slipping element can be missed and the same fault rebuilt back in.
mistakes.prevent: Air-check each clutch, brake and dog port with the valve body off and write down how each one behaves.

steps.title: Remove outer bell housing bolts
steps.action: Remove the bolts around the outside of the bell housing to case joint, leaving the one bolt that stays in throughout.
steps.why: One inner bolt also holds the output gear support to the bell housing and must stay until later.

mistakes.title: Mixing bell housing bolt lengths
mistakes.what: Pulls the perimeter bolts into one container.
mistakes.consequence: On assembly bolts go into the wrong holes, bottoming out or under-engaging threads in the aluminium case.
mistakes.prevent: Store the bolts in a template in their hole positions.

mistakes.title: Prying against a hidden bolt
mistakes.what: Starts prying the bell housing while a perimeter bolt is still in.
mistakes.consequence: The flange cracks or the sealing face is damaged, a costly housing or case replacement.
mistakes.prevent: Count the removed bolts against the service figure and check every hole with a light before prying.

steps.title: Remove inner bell housing bolts
steps.action: Remove the inner bell housing bolts, leaving the two marked bolts that retain the output gear support.
steps.mistake: Removing every inner bolt so the output support drops when the housing lifts.

mistakes.title: Removing every inner bolt
mistakes.what: Takes out all the inner bell housing bolts, including the ones that retain the output gear support.
mistakes.consequence: The output gear support and E clutch drop as the housing lifts, damaging the F dog, bearing or gear teeth.
mistakes.prevent: Leave the marked output support bolts in until the procedure calls for them.

steps.title: Lift bell housing off case
steps.action: Block the case bell-housing-up, pry at the proper pry points and lift the bell housing straight up; the E clutch, output gear support and filter come with it.
steps.why: Lifting straight protects the many tube O-rings and the stator support sealing rings.

mistakes.title: Prying at the wrong spot
mistakes.what: Drives a pry bar into the case-to-bell-housing joint anywhere it fits.
mistakes.consequence: The sealing faces are gouged and the case-to-converter-housing joint, one of JLR's listed leak points, weeps after assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Use only the designated pry points and lift evenly.

mistakes.title: Lifting the housing crooked
mistakes.what: Tilts the bell housing as it comes off the case.
mistakes.consequence: Tube O-ring bores and the stator support ring lands get scored, and the E clutch or output support can fall free.
mistakes.prevent: Lift straight up with the case blocked level, supporting the E clutch and output support as they rise.

steps.title: Remove gasket and tube seal
steps.action: Peel off the rubber-coated steel bell housing gasket and remove the tube seal that sits between case and bell housing.
steps.why: Both are single-use and the tube seal is easy to forget on reassembly.

mistakes.title: Leaving the old tube seal in
mistakes.what: Misses the old fluid port tube seal stuck in its bore.
mistakes.consequence: On assembly the new seal is stacked on the old one or left out, and the case-to-bell-housing circuit leaks; the fix means splitting the unit again.
mistakes.prevent: Remove the old tube seal as soon as the housing is off and put it with the scrap gasket.

mistakes.title: Scratching the joint faces
mistakes.what: Scrapes the gasket faces with a steel blade or abrasive disc.
mistakes.consequence: Scratches running across the face leak at the case-to-converter-housing joint, one of JLR's listed leak points.
mistakes.prevent: Clean the case and housing faces with solvent and a plastic scraper, never a blade or disc.

steps.title: Lift out the differential
steps.action: Lift the differential assembly out of the case.
steps.why: The final drive sits on top once the bell housing is off and must come out before the transfer gear.

mistakes.title: Mixing differential bearing races
mistakes.what: Lets the differential's tapered bearing cups and cones get swapped side to side.
mistakes.consequence: Bearings that were worn in as pairs run noisy and wear early when mismatched.
mistakes.prevent: Keep each cone with its own cup and tag them left and right.

steps.title: Lift out the transfer gear
steps.action: Remove the transfer gear (with its integral park gear) from its bearing.

mistakes.title: Knocking the park gear teeth
mistakes.what: Bangs the transfer gear against the case or bench while lifting it out.
mistakes.consequence: Chipped park gear teeth stop the pawl engaging cleanly, and the vehicle may not hold in Park.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the transfer gear straight out and set it on a clean, soft surface.

steps.title: Remove upper annulus and carrier
steps.action: Lift out the annulus and pinion carrier assembly that sits on top (Chrysler calls it the gear 4 annulus and carrier).

mistakes.title: Not tagging thrust washers and bearings
mistakes.what: Lifts out the annulus and carrier assemblies without tagging the thrust bearings, washers and spacers between them.
mistakes.consequence: Bearings go back in the wrong place or upside down, changing end play and leading to bearing failure.
mistakes.prevent: Tag every snap ring, washer, spacer and thrust bearing with its position and orientation as it comes out.

steps.title: Remove next annulus and carrier
steps.action: Lift out the next annulus and carrier assembly (Chrysler's gear 3 annulus and carrier gear).

mistakes.title: Letting a stuck bearing travel
mistakes.what: Doesn't check the underside of each assembly for a needle bearing stuck to it.
mistakes.consequence: The bearing ends up on the wrong part or is lost, and the stack-up is wrong on assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Turn each assembly over as it comes out and remove any bearing stuck to it.

steps.title: Pull transfer gear bearing off
steps.action: Use a two-jaw puller seated in the case reliefs to pull the transfer gear bearing off its case boss, spacing the puller with a socket if needed.
steps.why: The bearing blocks the D piston housing, so it must come off first; pulling on the cage ruins it.
steps.mistake: Hooking the puller on the roller cage instead of the inner race.

mistakes.title: Hooking the bearing cage
mistakes.what: Puts the puller jaws on the roller cage instead of the inner race.
mistakes.consequence: The cage bends and the rollers fall out, so the bearing is scrap and has to be replaced.
mistakes.prevent: Seat the jaws in the case reliefs under the inner race, spacing the puller with a socket if needed.

mistakes.title: Puller jaws on the case boss
mistakes.what: Lets the puller jaws bear on the case boss edge instead of sitting in the reliefs.
mistakes.consequence: The case boss is gouged or cracked, and the case is expensive to replace.
mistakes.prevent: Check jaw placement in the reliefs before turning the screw and stop if it binds.

steps.title: Compress D retainer, remove ring
steps.action: In an arbor press, compress the D piston retainer with the press tool and adapter and remove its snap ring.
steps.why: The Belleville spring is under real load; the retainer only moves about an eighth of an inch.

mistakes.title: Compressing the D retainer off-center
mistakes.what: Sets the press tool off-center so the D piston retainer tilts as it goes down.
mistakes.consequence: The retainer O-ring drops into the snap ring groove or is cut, and the D brake leaks on apply.
mistakes.prevent: Center the tool, compress evenly and only as far as the groove needs.
mistakes.detect: The O-ring visible in the snap ring groove after compression.

mistakes.title: Gouging the groove for a tabless ring
mistakes.what: Digs at the D snap ring, which has no pry tabs, with picks levered against the groove edge.
mistakes.consequence: The groove or retainer is damaged and the new ring will not seat fully.
mistakes.prevent: Relieve the ring's load in the press, rotate it to an opening and lift it without levering on the groove wall.

steps.title: Remove D piston and spring
steps.action: Lift out the D piston retainer, the aluminum D piston and its Belleville spring.

mistakes.title: Not noting Belleville spring direction
mistakes.what: Lifts out the D Belleville spring without marking which way its cone faced.
mistakes.consequence: Refitted upside down, it changes how the D piston applies and releases, causing drag or harsh apply.
mistakes.prevent: Mark the spring's up side and photograph it in place before removal.

mistakes.title: Scoring the aluminium D piston
mistakes.what: Pries the aluminium D piston out with a screwdriver.
mistakes.consequence: Scored piston or bore surfaces let D apply oil leak past the new seals, so D slips.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the piston out evenly by hand; replace it if the sealing surfaces are marked.

steps.title: Lift geartrain out by input shaft
steps.action: Lift the geartrain (annulus, B clutch pack and hub, input shaft) out of the case by the input shaft, never by the hub.
steps.why: Lifting by the hub pulls it out of the B clutch pack and drops the plates.
steps.mistake: Lifting the assembly by the hub so the B pack falls apart.

mistakes.title: Lifting the geartrain by the hub
mistakes.what: Grabs the geartrain by the B clutch hub instead of the input shaft.
mistakes.consequence: The hub pulls out of the B clutch pack and the plates fall out of order.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the whole geartrain only by the input shaft, keeping your hands off the B hub.

mistakes.title: Missing the bearing on the hub
mistakes.what: Doesn't check the bottom of the geartrain hub for the needle thrust bearing stuck to it.
mistakes.consequence: The bearing is lost or later goes back on the hub instead of the case bushing.
mistakes.prevent: Turn the geartrain over and remove the bearing to its tagged spot.

steps.title: Remove D brake pack
steps.action: Remove the D brake plates and frictions, keeping them in order.

mistakes.title: Mixing C and D plates
mistakes.what: Lays the D brake plates down with the C plates.
mistakes.consequence: Pack thickness and clearance change and the wear evidence for each pack is lost.
mistakes.prevent: Keep each pack in its own labelled tray in removal order.

steps.title: Remove C selective ring and pack
steps.action: Remove the C brake selective snap ring, then the C plates and frictions; tag the ring's thickness.
steps.why: The selective ring sets C clearance; knowing the old size speeds up shimming later.

mistakes.title: Not recording the selective ring
mistakes.what: Removes the C selective snap ring without measuring and tagging it.
mistakes.consequence: Shimming the C brake later starts from scratch and takes several tries.
mistakes.prevent: Measure the ring and write its thickness on the tag.

steps.title: Compress C spring, remove piston
steps.action: Fit the spring compressor plate over the C Belleville, compress it in the press, remove the snap ring, then lift out the spring and aluminum C piston.
steps.why: The C piston sits at the bottom of the case and is the last thing out; the spring is loaded hard enough to launch the ring.

mistakes.title: Spring tool slipping off
mistakes.what: Uses a C spring compressor that does not reach between the piston slots, or sets it crooked.
mistakes.consequence: The tool slips under load, launching the snap ring or damaging the piston and spring.
mistakes.prevent: Use the correct tool or a proven equivalent that sits between the piston slots, and compress straight.

mistakes.title: Prying the C piston from the case
mistakes.what: Levers the aluminium C piston out of its bore at the bottom of the case.
mistakes.consequence: The bore is part of the case, so scoring it means a C leak that only a new case fixes.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the piston out evenly by hand without tools touching the bore.

steps.title: Remove differential seals
steps.action: Drive out and discard the differential seals from both the case and the bell housing.

mistakes.title: Gouging the differential seal bores
mistakes.what: Drives the old differential seals out with a chisel that cuts into the bore.
mistakes.consequence: The new differential seals leak along the scratch and fluid drips at the halfshaft.
mistakes.prevent: Use a seal puller or drive from behind without touching the bore wall.

steps.title: Separate output support from housing
steps.action: Remove the remaining bolt holding the output gear support to the bell housing and lift the support away without dropping it.

mistakes.title: Dropping the output gear support
mistakes.what: Removes the last support bolt without holding the output gear support.
mistakes.consequence: It falls, damaging the F dog, its bearing or gear teeth.
mistakes.prevent: Hold the support while the bolt comes out and lift it away.

steps.title: Remove E clutch from housing
steps.action: Lift the E clutch hub and plates out in order, then lift the steel E drum off the stator support sealing rings.
steps.why: The drum carries the input speed sensor knockouts; bent tabs give a bad speed signal.

mistakes.title: Bending the speed sensor tabs
mistakes.what: Handles or stacks the steel E drum on its sensor knockouts.
mistakes.consequence: Bent tabs give the input speed sensor a bad signal, which shows up as shift faults and speed codes.
mistakes.prevent: Store the drum upright on a clean surface and check the tabs are straight.

mistakes.title: Dragging the drum over sealing rings
mistakes.what: Tilts the E drum as it comes off the stator support.
mistakes.consequence: The ring lands get scored, and new rings will leak E clutch apply oil.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the E drum straight up off the stator support without rocking it.

steps.title: Unbolt the stator support
steps.action: Unbolt the flanged stator support from the bell housing.

steps.title: Remove pump and drive chain
steps.action: Remove the pump drive chain and sprockets, noting their orientation, then lift the vane pump out of its pocket in the pump housing.
steps.why: The pump sits at the base of the pump housing inside the bell housing, off the input axis.

mistakes.title: Not marking chain and sprockets
mistakes.what: Removes the pump drive chain and sprockets without noting which face points out.
mistakes.consequence: A reused chain or sprocket refitted flipped runs on fresh wear surfaces, making noise and wearing fast.
mistakes.prevent: Mark the outer face of the chain and each sprocket before removal.

mistakes.title: Prying the pump from its pocket
mistakes.what: Levers the vane pump out of its pocket with a screwdriver against the housing.
mistakes.consequence: The pocket in the pump housing is damaged, and that housing is part of the bell housing assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Lift the pump out evenly by its body, working it up a little at each side.

steps.title: Remove filter from pump housing
steps.action: Pull the filter outlet neck out of the pump housing and discard the filter and its O-rings.
steps.why: There is no pan to reach the filter from outside, so it is only changed during a teardown.

mistakes.title: Leaving the filter O-ring behind
mistakes.what: Pulls the filter but leaves its outlet neck O-ring in the pump housing bore.
mistakes.consequence: The new filter will not seat over the old ring and the pump draws air, aerating the fluid and dropping pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Check the bore is empty and clean after pulling the filter.

steps.title: Remove converter hub seal
steps.action: Remove the snap ring and drive out the converter hub seal; check the hub support bearing.
steps.why: The converter hub runs in a bearing, not a bushing, so check it for roughness while it is exposed.

mistakes.title: Hitting the hub bearing
mistakes.what: Drives the converter hub seal out with a punch that strikes the hub support bearing behind it.
mistakes.consequence: The bearing is damaged, runs rough and wears the hub seal.
mistakes.prevent: Remove the snap ring and pull the seal without contacting the bearing.

steps.title: Split B drum from geartrain
steps.action: Separate the input shaft and B clutch drum from the planetary 3/4 housing.

mistakes.title: Forcing the A dog splines apart
mistakes.what: Hammers or levers the input shaft out of the 3-sun/4-ring splines.
mistakes.consequence: The A dog teeth chip, and the fix is usually a complete input shaft assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Separate the parts straight along their axis by hand; if they bind, find why.

steps.title: Disassemble the B clutch
steps.action: Compress the B Belleville spring, remove the snap ring and remove the inverted pack, cushion plate and aluminum piston.
steps.why: The B pack is inverted (frictions with outside teeth), so note the stack order.

mistakes.title: Losing the inverted B pack order
mistakes.what: Takes the B pack apart without recording the stack order of its outside-toothed frictions, steels and cushion plate.
mistakes.consequence: The pack is rebuilt in the conventional order and will not work correctly.
mistakes.prevent: Photograph and lay out the pack in removal order.

mistakes.title: Uneven B spring compression
mistakes.what: Compresses the B Belleville spring with the tool off-center.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminium B piston cocks in its bore and its seals or the bore surface are damaged.
mistakes.prevent: Center the compressor on the B spring and bring it down slowly and evenly.

steps.title: Disassemble the E clutch
steps.action: Compress the E Belleville spring, remove its retainer and the bonded piston from the steel drum.

mistakes.title: Trying to reseal the bonded piston
mistakes.what: Attempts to peel or replace the seal on the bonded E piston.
mistakes.consequence: The bonded seal cannot be renewed separately, so the piston is ruined.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the bonded piston as a unit and replace the whole piston if the seal is damaged.

steps.title: Strip output support and F dog
steps.action: Remove the output gear nut, bearing and gear from the support, then remove the F dog sleeve and its double-acting piston and cover.
steps.why: The F dog grounds the shared sun of sets 1 and 2 to this support.

mistakes.title: Mixing F dog seal sides
mistakes.what: Strips the double-acting F dog piston and cover without noting which seals sit on the apply and release sides.
mistakes.consequence: On rebuild the F dog will not shuttle both ways, giving dog position faults and wrong gear selection.
mistakes.prevent: Lay out the F dog parts in order and note which seal goes where.

steps.title: Separate planetary sets 3 and 4
steps.action: Release the snap ring joining the C and D hubs and separate planetary sets 3 and 4 from their shared aluminum housing.

mistakes.title: Prying the shared housing apart
mistakes.what: Levers between sets 3 and 4 to split their shared aluminium housing.
mistakes.consequence: The housing or the 3-sun/4-ring splines the A dog engages are damaged.
mistakes.prevent: Release the snap ring fully and separate the sets straight by hand.

steps.title: Mark and dismantle the pump
steps.action: Mark every pump piece, compress the dished back plate with clamps, remove the clip and take the pump apart.
steps.why: The parts only work one way round; unmarked vanes and plates are hard to place again.
steps.mistake: Disassembling the pump without marking the parts' orientation.

mistakes.title: Disassembling the pump unmarked
mistakes.what: Takes the pump apart without marking each piece's orientation.
mistakes.consequence: The parts go back in the wrong way round and the pump loses output or wears out quickly.
mistakes.prevent: Mark every plate, ring and the rotor face before the clip comes off.

mistakes.title: Releasing the dished plate unclamped
mistakes.what: Removes the pump clip without compressing the dished back plate.
mistakes.consequence: The preloaded plate springs the clip out, damaging its groove or the plate.
mistakes.prevent: Clamp the plate down before removing the clip and release the clamp slowly.

mistakes.title: Mixing vanes between slots
mistakes.what: Tips the vanes out together and loses which slot and which way each came from.
mistakes.consequence: Worn-in vanes in different slots stick or leak, reducing pump output.
mistakes.prevent: Note each vane's position and edge direction, or replace the vane set.

steps.title: Strip the valve body
steps.action: Remove the solenoids in their marked order, separate the valve body halves, and lay out valves, springs and sleeves by bore.

mistakes.title: Losing small valve body parts
mistakes.what: Separates the valve body halves over an open bench.
mistakes.consequence: Loose springs, retainers and plugs fall out, and a missing or misplaced one changes how a circuit regulates.
mistakes.prevent: Split the halves over a tray, slowly, and lay each part out in bore order.

mistakes.title: Mixing springs between bores
mistakes.what: Puts all valve springs in one cup.
mistakes.consequence: Similar-looking springs swap bores and change regulated pressure, causing harsh or soft shifts.
mistakes.prevent: Lay out valves and springs in bore order on a labelled board.

mistakes.title: Forcing a stuck valve out
mistakes.what: Taps or pries a stuck valve out of its bore.
mistakes.consequence: The aluminium bore is scored and the valve body needs a reamed oversize repair or replacement.
mistakes.prevent: Clean and free a stuck valve gently; if it will not come free, plan an oversize repair.

steps.title: Clean all parts and passages
steps.action: Wash every part in clean solvent, blow passages dry with air, and keep each subassembly's parts together.

mistakes.title: Leaving lint in passages
mistakes.what: Dries valve body parts and case passages with shop rags.
mistakes.consequence: Lint lodges in a valve bore or solenoid screen and sticks a valve on the first drive.
mistakes.prevent: Blow parts dry with clean air and keep rags away from hydraulic parts.

mistakes.title: Not blowing out every passage
mistakes.what: Washes parts in the tank but doesn't blow through every feed passage and tube bore.
mistakes.consequence: Debris left in a passage plugs a solenoid or valve after assembly.
mistakes.prevent: Blow through each passage with clean air and watch for flow at the other end.

steps.title: Inspect A dog splines
steps.action: Check the A dog sleeve and its mating sun/ring gear splines for rounding, chipping and heat marks, and check that the sleeve slides freely.
steps.why: The sleeve usually wears before the gears; spline damage here causes loss of forward gears.

mistakes.title: Passing rounded dog teeth
mistakes.what: Accepts A dog teeth with slight rounding or chipped edges.
mistakes.consequence: Rounded teeth ratchet or pop out under load and the dog clutch fault returns soon after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Reject any A dog sleeve or gear with rounded, chipped or heat-marked teeth.

mistakes.title: Checking only the sleeve
mistakes.what: Inspects the A dog sleeve but not the mating spline on the 3-sun/4-ring gear.
mistakes.consequence: A worn spline on the mating gear chews up a new sleeve and the dog fault returns.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the 3-sun/4-ring spline as closely as the sleeve and reject either if worn.

mistakes.title: Not measuring sleeve travel
mistakes.what: Judges A dog sleeve freedom by feel alone.
mistakes.consequence: A sleeve that binds partway passes on the bench and fails to complete its travel in the vehicle.
mistakes.prevent: Slide the sleeve through its full range and confirm the travel with a dial caliper.

steps.title: Check A dog sensing screw
steps.action: Check that the small screw holding the A dog sensing valve plate is tight and its head is intact.
steps.why: A loose or broken screw stops the piston's full travel, gives erratic sensor readings and grinds the dog.
steps.mistake: Assuming the A dog is fine because the splines look good.

mistakes.title: Trusting good-looking splines
mistakes.what: Assumes the A dog is fine because the splines look good and skips the sensing valve screw.
mistakes.consequence: A loose or broken sensing plate screw stops full piston travel, gives erratic sensor readings and grinds the dog.
mistakes.prevent: Check the screw is tight and intact on every unit, whatever the splines look like.

mistakes.title: Retightening a damaged screw
mistakes.what: Snugs up a loose sensing plate screw whose head is damaged and reuses the shaft.
mistakes.consequence: The damaged screw backs out again in service and the A dog failure repeats.
mistakes.prevent: Treat a loose or damaged screw as a failed input shaft and replace the assembly.

mistakes.title: Mistaking the loose pin for damage
mistakes.what: Sees the hardened pin through the sensing valve move freely and thinks it is broken.
mistakes.consequence: Good parts get replaced; that pin is loosely held by design.
mistakes.prevent: Know that the pin passes loosely through the valve and judge the screw and travel instead.

steps.title: Air-test A dog travel
steps.action: Hold the input shaft upright, apply air to the apply side and confirm the sleeve travels fully with little leakage, then confirm it returns.
steps.why: If it fails, the fix is a complete input shaft assembly; the parts are not serviced separately.

mistakes.title: Passing a slow return
mistakes.what: Accepts an A dog that applies on air but returns slowly or not fully.
mistakes.consequence: In the vehicle the sleeve does not release on time, setting clutch position errors such as P0810.
mistakes.prevent: Require full travel both ways with little leakage, holding the shaft upright as you test.

mistakes.title: Fitting the wrong input shaft
mistakes.what: Replaces a failed input shaft with one listed for the Chrysler 948TE.
mistakes.consequence: Chrysler shafts have no orificed tip while other applications do, so the A dog circuit behaves differently.
mistakes.prevent: Match the replacement shaft to the 9HP48 variant and compare the tip with the old shaft before fitting.

steps.title: Inspect F dog and sun
steps.action: Check the F dog sleeve, its two sealing rings and the synchro splines on the shared sun gear of sets 1 and 2.

mistakes.title: Ignoring F dog sealing rings
mistakes.what: Reuses the F dog sealing rings because they look intact.
mistakes.consequence: Leaking rings slow the F dog's travel and its position fault returns.
mistakes.prevent: Replace the F dog rings and check their grooves.

mistakes.title: Missing a blocked sensing hole
mistakes.what: Doesn't clean and check the F dog sensing hole.
mistakes.consequence: With the hole blocked, the pressure sensor cannot tell when the F dog has finished moving, and the TCM sets position faults.
mistakes.prevent: Blow through the sensing hole and confirm it is clear.

mistakes.title: Passing worn sun gear splines
mistakes.what: Doesn't inspect the dog splines on the shared sun of sets 1 and 2.
mistakes.consequence: A worn sun spline ratchets against a new F dog sleeve.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the sun splines as closely as the sleeve.

steps.title: Bench-test dog pressure sensor
steps.action: Power the dog clutch pressure sensor from a bench supply and apply air to confirm its output changes; an ohmmeter will not test it.
steps.why: The TCM uses this sensor to know when either dog has finished moving.

spec.note: approximate pressure the sensor sees while a dog piston is moving; drops to 0 at full travel (948TE)

mistakes.title: Testing the sensor with an ohmmeter
mistakes.what: Checks the dog clutch pressure sensor with an ohmmeter.
mistakes.consequence: It is a powered Hall-effect sensor, so the reading means nothing and a good sensor is scrapped or a bad one passed.
mistakes.prevent: Power it from a bench supply, apply air and watch the output change.

mistakes.title: Skipping the sensor test
mistakes.what: Reinstalls the original sensor untested after a dog clutch fault.
mistakes.consequence: If the sensor was the fault, dog position codes come back and the valve body has to come off again.
mistakes.prevent: Bench-test the dog pressure sensor on every rebuild done for a dog-related fault.

steps.title: Inspect valve body bores
steps.action: Check the pressure regulator, the SV-SP valve and the A/F dog plunger valve sleeves for bore wear and sticking.
steps.why: Worn plunger sleeves let dog clutch pressure overlap or exhaust early; SV-SP wear upsets line pressure.

mistakes.title: Overlooking the SV-SP valve
mistakes.what: Checks the pressure regulator bore but not the SV-SP valve that feeds it.
mistakes.consequence: The SV-SP valve feeds the regulator, so its wear upsets line pressure, shift quality and clutch life.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect and vacuum-test the SV-SP bore along with the pressure regulator bores.

mistakes.title: Judging bores by feel only
mistakes.what: Decides a valve bore is fine because the valve slides freely.
mistakes.consequence: Bore wear that leaks pressure goes undetected and line pressure regulation stays poor.
mistakes.prevent: Vacuum-test the specified bores and fix any that will not hold.
mistakes.detect: A bore that will not hold vacuum at its test port.

mistakes.title: Passing scratched plunger sleeves
mistakes.what: Reuses A/F dog plunger valve sleeves with visible scratches.
mistakes.consequence: Worn sleeves let dog clutch pressure overlap or exhaust early, giving delayed engagement and loss of higher gears.
mistakes.prevent: Replace the plunger valves and sleeves when the sleeve bore or valve shows wear.

steps.title: Inspect pump, chain, sprockets
steps.action: Check the vane pump faces, vanes and rotor, the chain for stretch, and the drive gear's four flats where the converter hub engages.

mistakes.title: Reusing a stretched pump chain
mistakes.what: Refits the pump drive chain without checking it for stretch and wear.
mistakes.consequence: A worn pump chain whines or slaps and can upset how steadily the pump is driven.
mistakes.prevent: Compare the chain with a new one and replace it if it is stretched.

mistakes.title: Missing worn drive flats
mistakes.what: Doesn't check the four flats on the pump drive gear where the converter hub engages.
mistakes.consequence: Worn flats slip or break under load, and the pump stops delivering.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the flats and the converter hub drive for wear and replace worn parts.

mistakes.title: Ignoring scored pump faces
mistakes.what: Reuses a pump with scored faces or a worn rotor.
mistakes.consequence: Pump output drops, and line pressure is low at hot idle.
mistakes.prevent: Check the pump faces, rotor and vanes and replace the pump if they are scored.

steps.title: Inspect planetaries and thrust bearings
steps.action: Spin each planetary pinion for roughness and end play, and check every needle thrust bearing and washer.

mistakes.title: Passing heat-blued pinions
mistakes.what: Reuses a carrier with discoloured pinions or rough-spinning gears.
mistakes.consequence: Overheated pinions fail early and send needles and metal through the new unit.
mistakes.prevent: Spin each pinion and check end play; replace a carrier with any roughness or heat marks.

mistakes.title: Reusing pitted thrust bearings
mistakes.what: Reuses needle thrust bearings with pitting or flat spots.
mistakes.consequence: Pitted needle bearings get noisy and can break up, spreading metal through the geartrain.
mistakes.prevent: Replace any needle thrust bearing that feels rough when spun or shows marks on its races.

steps.title: Inspect bushings and ring lands
steps.action: Check bushings, sealing ring grooves, the pressed-in steel sealing-ring support in the case and the stator support ring lands.

mistakes.title: Missing worn ring grooves
mistakes.what: Fits new sealing rings into worn ring grooves.
mistakes.consequence: The rings leak in worn grooves, and the clutch they feed slips.
mistakes.prevent: Check each groove's sides for steps and wear before fitting new rings.

mistakes.title: Ignoring the pressed-in ring support
mistakes.what: Doesn't check the steel sealing-ring support pressed into the case.
mistakes.consequence: A loose or worn support leaks past its rings and starves the circuit.
mistakes.prevent: Check the support for movement and wear with the case bare.

steps.title: Inspect pistons, springs, drums
steps.action: Check the C, D and B aluminum pistons, the bonded E piston, every Belleville spring and the drum splines for cracks, distortion and wear.

mistakes.title: Reusing a tired Belleville spring
mistakes.what: Reuses a Belleville spring without comparing its cone height with a new one.
mistakes.consequence: A flattened spring releases its piston slowly, giving drag and heat in that pack.
mistakes.prevent: Compare each spring with a new part and replace any that have lost height or show cracks.

mistakes.title: Missing a cracked piston
mistakes.what: Washes an aluminium piston and puts it back without close inspection.
mistakes.consequence: A hairline crack leaks apply oil, and the pack slips and burns.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect each piston under bright light and replace any with cracks or nicks.

mistakes.title: Ignoring notched drum splines
mistakes.what: Passes a drum with notches worn into its splines.
mistakes.consequence: Plates hang in the notches instead of sliding freely, causing drag or harsh apply.
mistakes.prevent: Run a fingernail across each drum spline and replace any drum with notches.

steps.title: Inspect final drive and park
steps.action: Check transfer gear and differential tapered bearings, the park gear teeth and pawl, and the park rod cam.

mistakes.title: Passing a worn park pawl
mistakes.what: Reuses a park pawl or park gear with worn engagement faces.
mistakes.consequence: The pawl can ratchet out of the park gear, so the vehicle may roll while in Park.
mistakes.prevent: Check the pawl nose and park gear teeth closely and replace worn parts.

mistakes.title: Reusing pitted final drive bearings
mistakes.what: Puts pitted transfer gear or differential tapered bearings back in.
mistakes.consequence: The final drive whines on the road and needs a second teardown to replace the bearings.
mistakes.prevent: Replace any transfer gear or differential tapered bearing that is rough, pitted or discoloured.

mistakes.title: Not checking park rod movement
mistakes.what: Doesn't check the park rod and cam for free movement.
mistakes.consequence: A sticky park linkage contributes to stuck-in-Park complaints after the rebuild.
mistakes.prevent: Work the linkage through its range by hand and check it returns cleanly.

steps.title: Check sensors and connector plate
steps.action: Check speed sensors, range sensor and connector plate wiring for chafing, heat damage and bad terminals.

mistakes.title: Not checking terminal crimps
mistakes.what: Looks at the internal wiring but doesn't test the terminal crimps.
mistakes.consequence: Poor crimps in the transmission harness caused sudden shifts to neutral on early units, a safety recall.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect and gently pull-test each terminal and replace any harness section with a loose crimp.

mistakes.title: Ignoring heat-damaged wiring
mistakes.what: Passes connector plate wiring with brittle or chafed insulation.
mistakes.consequence: Brittle or chafed wiring shorts or opens later, giving intermittent sensor and solenoid codes.
mistakes.prevent: Replace the connector plate or harness section when the insulation is damaged.

steps.title: Judge the torque converter
steps.action: Decide whether the converter can be reused or should go to a converter rebuilder or be replaced with a remanufactured unit.
steps.why: Lockup is used in every gear, so a worn lockup clutch shows up as shudder; debris left in it re-contaminates the new parts.

mistakes.title: Reusing a contaminated converter
mistakes.what: Puts the old converter back after a failure that made debris.
mistakes.consequence: Debris trapped inside the converter washes out into the new frictions, bushings and valve body.
mistakes.prevent: Send the converter out for cleaning and rebuild, or replace it, when the fluid showed debris.

mistakes.title: Ignoring lockup shudder history
mistakes.what: Reuses the converter without asking about shudder before the rebuild.
mistakes.consequence: Lockup is used in every gear, so a worn lockup clutch shudders after the rebuild and gets blamed on it.
mistakes.prevent: Ask about shudder and send the converter out if there was any.

mistakes.title: Not checking the hub drive
mistakes.what: Doesn't inspect the converter hub's drive flats and seal surface.
mistakes.consequence: A worn hub slips in the pump drive or leaks past the new seal.
mistakes.prevent: Inspect the hub flats and sealing surface and replace the converter if they are worn.

steps.title: Sort replace versus reuse
steps.action: Set aside for replacement all frictions, seals, O-rings, gaskets, the filter and converter nuts; keep hard parts that passed inspection.
steps.why: Every tube O-ring, the bell housing gasket and the tube seal are single-use.
steps.mistake: Reusing tube O-rings that look fine but have taken a set.

mistakes.title: Reusing tube O-rings
mistakes.what: Reuses tube O-rings that look fine but have taken a set.
mistakes.consequence: A hardened O-ring leaks a clutch or lube feed, causing slip or wear.
mistakes.prevent: Replace every tube O-ring and gasket, whatever they look like.

mistakes.title: Keeping the old C snap ring
mistakes.what: Puts the C piston snap ring back in the reuse pile.
mistakes.consequence: FCA's C snap ring fix used a new ring, and a ring that dislodges leaves C stuck on.
mistakes.prevent: Treat the C piston snap ring as single-use and order a new one with the kit.

mistakes.title: Using a 948TE kit unchecked
mistakes.what: Orders a rebuild kit listed for the 948TE and assumes it all fits the JLR 9HP48.
mistakes.consequence: Some parts differ, such as plunger valve diameters by park type, so the wrong part goes in.
mistakes.prevent: Check each kit part against the old one before assembly.

steps.title: Rebuild valve body bores
steps.action: Fit replacement valves and sleeves where bores are worn, then reassemble the halves with the manual valve rotated to line up with its notches.
steps.why: A misaligned manual valve leaves the selector and valve body out of step.
steps.mistake: Reassembling the valve body with the manual valve turned wrong.

mistakes.title: Manual valve turned wrong
mistakes.what: Reassembles the valve body with the manual valve rotated off its notches.
mistakes.consequence: The selector and valve body are out of step and park or gear selection is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Line the manual valve up with its notches and check it before closing the valve body.

mistakes.title: Oversize valve without reaming
mistakes.what: Drops an oversize repair valve into a worn bore without reaming it.
mistakes.consequence: The valve does not fit or still leaks, and line pressure stays wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Ream the bore with the kit's tool kit, clean it, then fit the valve.

mistakes.title: Wrong plunger size for park type
mistakes.what: Fits A/F dog plunger valves without checking whether the valve body is park-by-wire or park-by-cable.
mistakes.consequence: The two use different plunger diameters, so the wrong valve leaks or binds.
mistakes.prevent: Measure the old plunger and match the kit to it.

steps.title: Refit solenoids and connector plate
steps.action: Install each solenoid in its marked bore and refit the connector plate, routing the sensor wires as photographed.

mistakes.title: Solenoid in the wrong bore
mistakes.what: Installs a solenoid in a bore other than the one it came from.
mistakes.consequence: The solenoid drives the wrong element, giving harsh shifts, wrong gears or a tie-up.
mistakes.prevent: Match each solenoid to the bore marked at teardown before you push it in.

mistakes.title: Pinching a solenoid O-ring
mistakes.what: Pushes a solenoid into its bore with a dry or rolled O-ring.
mistakes.consequence: The cut O-ring leaks control pressure, and the element that solenoid controls slips.
mistakes.prevent: Lube each solenoid O-ring and push the solenoid in straight, not at an angle.

mistakes.title: Routing wires into a pinch point
mistakes.what: Routes the connector plate wires differently from the photos.
mistakes.consequence: The cover or valve body pinches a wire, causing sensor or solenoid codes.
mistakes.prevent: Route every connector plate wire exactly as the teardown photos show.

steps.title: Reassemble the oil pump
steps.action: Reassemble the pump parts in their marked positions, compress the dished back plate in the press and fit the clip.
steps.why: The dished plate preloads the pump and must face the right way.

mistakes.title: Dished plate upside down
mistakes.what: Fits the dished back plate the wrong way up.
mistakes.consequence: The pump loses its built-in preload, so its output drops and line pressure suffers.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the plate the way it was marked and confirm it before clamping.

mistakes.title: Pump clip not fully seated
mistakes.what: Releases the press before the pump clip is fully in its groove.
mistakes.consequence: The pump can come apart in service and lose pressure, burning every pack.
mistakes.prevent: Recompress the plate and check the clip is fully seated all round.

steps.title: Install pump and chain
steps.action: Seat the pump with new O-rings in the pump housing, lining up its raised lip, then fit the chain and sprockets.
steps.why: The pump body only seats one way; 180 degrees off and it will not sit down.
steps.mistake: Seating the pump body rotated 180 degrees.

mistakes.title: Pump seated 180 degrees off
mistakes.what: Tries to seat the pump with its raised lip turned the wrong way.
mistakes.consequence: It will not sit down, and forcing it damages the pump or its pocket.
mistakes.prevent: Line up the raised lip with its mating feature before pressing.

mistakes.title: Rolling the pump O-ring
mistakes.what: Seats the pump with a dry O-ring that rolls in the pocket.
mistakes.consequence: The pump draws air past the rolled O-ring, aerating the fluid and dropping pressure.
mistakes.prevent: Lube the pump O-rings and press the pump in straight so they cannot roll.

mistakes.title: Chain refitted flipped
mistakes.what: Refits a reused chain with its marked face turned in.
mistakes.consequence: The chain runs on fresh wear surfaces, gets noisy and wears fast.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the chain with its mark facing out as recorded.

steps.title: Fit new filter and seal
steps.action: Push the new filter's outlet neck with new O-rings into the pump housing, and install a new converter hub seal and its snap ring.

mistakes.title: Filter neck not fully home
mistakes.what: Leaves the filter outlet neck short of fully seated in the pump housing.
mistakes.consequence: Air leaks in at the filter neck, so the fluid aerates and pressure drops under load.
mistakes.prevent: Push the neck fully home with lubed O-rings and check it is seated.

mistakes.title: Hub seal driven crooked
mistakes.what: Drives the converter hub seal in at an angle or too deep.
mistakes.consequence: The seal leaks at the converter and the unit has to come out again.
mistakes.prevent: Drive the seal square with the correct installer to its stop.

mistakes.title: Forgetting the seal snap ring
mistakes.what: Leaves out the hub seal's snap ring.
mistakes.consequence: The hub seal walks out of its bore and the unit dumps fluid at the converter.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the hub seal snap ring and run a pick around it to check it is seated.

steps.title: Bolt in the stator support
steps.action: Bolt the stator support to the bell housing with new sealing rings.

mistakes.title: Cutting the support sealing rings
mistakes.what: Over-stretches or cuts the stator support sealing rings during install.
mistakes.consequence: The E clutch leaks apply oil, slipping in gears 4 to 9.
mistakes.prevent: Stretch the rings gently, size them down after fitting, and coat with assembly lube.

steps.title: Rebuild E clutch drum
steps.action: Fit the bonded piston, Belleville spring and retainer, then the segmented frictions, steels and cushion spring, and the selective snap ring.

mistakes.title: Installing frictions dry
mistakes.what: Stacks new E clutch frictions without soaking them.
mistakes.consequence: Dry E frictions overheat and glaze on the first shifts, shortening the new pack's life.
mistakes.prevent: Soak every new E friction in LifeguardFluid 9 before stacking it.

mistakes.title: Cushion spring left out
mistakes.what: Builds the E pack without the cushion spring or puts it in the wrong place.
mistakes.consequence: The E clutch applies harshly and the clearance check is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Fit the cushion spring where the stack layout shows.

steps.title: Check E clutch clearance
steps.action: Load the pack with the specified force and measure clearance; change the selective snap ring until it is in range.

spec.note: with 45 lb on the pack; selective snap ring (948TE/9HP48 data via GEARS)

steps.mistake: Measuring with no load on a cushioned pack and reading it as too loose.

mistakes.title: Measuring an unloaded cushioned pack
mistakes.what: Measures E clearance with no load on the pack.
mistakes.consequence: Cushioned packs compress under load, so the wrong selective ring is chosen and E slips or drags.
mistakes.prevent: Put the specified load on the E pack with a force gauge before taking the reading.

mistakes.title: Forcing a feeler gauge in
mistakes.what: Tries to measure E clearance with a feeler gauge.
mistakes.consequence: There is no room behind the E backing plate, so a feeler reading is false.
mistakes.prevent: Use the two-step method: free clearance first, then dial indicator deflection under load.

mistakes.title: Not seating the pack first
mistakes.what: Measures right after stacking.
mistakes.consequence: A new pack settles after the first applies, so the clearance grows past what you measured.
mistakes.prevent: Apply the clutch several times with air to settle the stack, then measure.

steps.title: Rebuild B clutch drum
steps.action: Fit the aluminum piston and Belleville spring, then stack the inverted pack with its cushion plate and the selective backing plate.

mistakes.title: Stacking the B pack conventionally
mistakes.what: Builds the B pack in the usual friction-on-hub order instead of its inverted layout with outside-toothed frictions.
mistakes.consequence: The frictions cannot engage their drum splines as designed, so B will not hold in reverse, 3rd, 5th or 9th.
mistakes.prevent: Rebuild the B stack from the layout photos taken at teardown, checking which part carries the outside teeth.

mistakes.title: B cushion plate at the wrong end
mistakes.what: Puts the B cushion plate at the wrong end of the stack or leaves it out.
mistakes.consequence: The B apply becomes harsh and the clearance reading taken next no longer means anything.
mistakes.prevent: Place the cushion plate where the teardown photos show it, before stacking the frictions.

steps.title: Check B clutch clearance
steps.action: Load the pack with the specified force, measure clearance and pick the backing plate that puts it in range for that friction count.

spec.note: with three double-sided plus two single-sided frictions; 0.040–0.060 in with two plus two; 45 lb load; selective backing plate (GEARS)

mistakes.title: Wrong B spec for friction count
mistakes.what: Measures B clearance against the spec for the other friction count.
mistakes.consequence: B has two specs depending on how many frictions the pack holds, so the wrong one leaves the pack too tight or too loose.
mistakes.prevent: Count the double- and single-sided frictions in the pack and pick the spec that matches that count.

mistakes.title: Measuring B with the input shaft in
mistakes.what: Measures B clearance with the input shaft already installed in the drum.
mistakes.consequence: The shaft gets in the way of the press and the gauge, so the backing plate you choose is wrong.
mistakes.prevent: Assemble the B housing, piston and pack with the input shaft left out, then load and measure.

steps.title: Rebuild output support and F dog
steps.action: Fit the F dog piston and cover with new seals, slide on the sleeve, then refit the output gear, bearing and nut to the support.

mistakes.title: Cutting F dog piston seals
mistakes.what: Fits the F dog piston and cover seals dry or stretches them over sharp edges.
mistakes.consequence: A cut seal lets the double-acting F dog leak, so it moves slowly or stops partway and sets position faults.
mistakes.prevent: Lube each seal, stretch it evenly, size it down after fitting and check it is not twisted.

mistakes.title: Output gear nut left loose
mistakes.what: Runs the output gear nut down by feel and does not torque or lock it to the service data.
mistakes.consequence: The gear and its bearing loosen on the support, giving gear whine and tooth damage later on.
mistakes.prevent: Torque the nut to the service figure and secure it with the locking method the service data specifies.

steps.title: Air-check F dog shuttle
steps.action: Apply air to the F dog apply and release ports and confirm the sleeve shuttles fully both ways.

spec.note: approximate air pressure needed before the F dog shuttles (GEARS)

mistakes.title: Testing the F dog with too little air
mistakes.what: Air-checks the rebuilt F dog at low pressure and sees no movement.
mistakes.consequence: A good F dog looks seized and gets stripped down again for nothing.
